Exploring the abundance table

Introduction

This report explores the abundance table table.tsv:

  • rows = taxa, labeled with their full taxonomic lineage (e.g. k__Bacteria,p__Firmicutes,...,g__Lactobacillus)
  • columns = samples (sequencing runs named ERR...)
  • values = raw abundance counts

We will import the data, reshape it to tidy format, parse the taxonomy, look at library sizes and community composition, and finish with a few plots.

Import the data

read_tsv() parses the tab-separated file. The first column is called #Taxon in the header, so we rename it to Taxon right away (backticks are needed because the name starts with #).

counts <- read_tsv("table.tsv") |>
  rename(Taxon = `#Taxon`)

cat("Table dimensions:", nrow(counts), "taxa x", ncol(counts) - 1, "samples\n")
## Table dimensions: 102 taxa x 29 samples
counts |> slice(1:5, 1:5)
## # A tibble: 10 × 30

Tidy the data

For most analyses (and for ggplot2) it is convenient to have one row per (taxon, sample) combination: this is the long or tidy format. pivot_longer() stacks all sample columns into two new columns: Sample (the former column name) and Count (the value).

tidy_counts <- counts |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Taxon,
    names_to = "Sample",
    values_to = "Count"
  )

tidy_counts
## # A tibble: 2,958 × 3
##    Taxon           Sample      Count
##    <chr>           <chr>       <dbl>
##  1 u__unclassified ERR17070056  1503
##  2 u__unclassified ERR17070057  1683
##  3 u__unclassified ERR17070058  1107
##  4 u__unclassified ERR17070059  1440
##  5 u__unclassified ERR17070060  1702
##  6 u__unclassified ERR17070061  1634
##  7 u__unclassified ERR17070062  1403
##  8 u__unclassified ERR17070063  1637
##  9 u__unclassified ERR17070064  1042
## 10 u__unclassified ERR17070065  1719
## # ℹ 2,948 more rows

The wide table of 102 taxa x 29 samples becomes 2958 rows, of which 2009 (~68%) are nonzero.

Parse the taxonomy

Row labels are full lineage strings. We extract the rank prefixes (p__ = phylum, g__ = genus, …) with regular expressions:

  • str_extract(Taxon, "g__[^,]+") finds the g__Genus token ([^,]+ = any characters up to the next comma)
  • str_remove(..., "g__") strips the prefix
  • replace_na(...) labels rows that lack the rank (e.g. u__unclassified)
tidy_counts <- tidy_counts |>
  mutate(
    Phylum = str_extract(Taxon, "p__[^,]+") |> str_remove("p__") |>
      replace_na("unclassified"),
    Genus  = str_extract(Taxon, "g__[^,]+") |> str_remove("g__") |>
      replace_na("unclassified")
  )

tidy_counts
## # A tibble: 2,958 × 5
##    Taxon           Sample      Count Phylum       Genus       
##    <chr>           <chr>       <dbl> <chr>        <chr>       
##  1 u__unclassified ERR17070056  1503 unclassified unclassified
##  2 u__unclassified ERR17070057  1683 unclassified unclassified
##  3 u__unclassified ERR17070058  1107 unclassified unclassified
##  4 u__unclassified ERR17070059  1440 unclassified unclassified
##  5 u__unclassified ERR17070060  1702 unclassified unclassified
##  6 u__unclassified ERR17070061  1634 unclassified unclassified
##  7 u__unclassified ERR17070062  1403 unclassified unclassified
##  8 u__unclassified ERR17070063  1637 unclassified unclassified
##  9 u__unclassified ERR17070064  1042 unclassified unclassified
## 10 u__unclassified ERR17070065  1719 unclassified unclassified

Exploration

Library sizes

The library size is the total number of counts of a sample. Samples can differ enormously in sequencing depth, which matters when comparing them — hence the relative abundances used later.

library_sizes <- tidy_counts |>
  summarise(Total = sum(Count), .by = Sample) |>
  arrange(desc(Total))

library_sizes
## # A tibble: 29 × 2
##    Sample       Total
##    <chr>        <dbl>
##  1 ERR17070069 357794
##  2 ERR17070075 319095
##  3 ERR17070079 316872
##  4 ERR17070070 316414
##  5 ERR17070072 305957
##  6 ERR17070068 297616
##  7 ERR17070074 291879
##  8 ERR17070065 279290
##  9 ERR17070078 279086
## 10 ERR17070073 277663
## # ℹ 19 more rows

The largest sample (ERR17070069, 357,794 counts) has more than 100x the reads of the smallest one (2,744 counts).

Composition by phylum

Collapsing all taxa that share the same phylum gives the broadest picture of the community:

by_phylum <- tidy_counts |>
  summarise(Total = sum(Count), .by = Phylum) |>
  arrange(desc(Total)) |>
  mutate(Percent = round(100 * Total / sum(Total), 2))

by_phylum
## # A tibble: 6 × 3
##   Phylum             Total Percent
##   <chr>              <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 Firmicutes       5900601   89.2 
## 2 Proteobacteria    607522    9.19
## 3 unclassified       45636    0.69
## 4 Actinobacteriota   34424    0.52
## 5 Bacteroidota       23851    0.36
## 6 Patescibacteria      448    0.01

The community is dominated by Firmicutes (~89%), followed by Proteobacteria (~9%): a composition typical of fermented-food / dairy-type microbiomes.

Top genera

top_genera <- tidy_counts |>
  summarise(Total = sum(Count), .by = Genus) |>
  arrange(desc(Total)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

top_genera
## # A tibble: 10 × 2
##    Genus             Total
##    <chr>             <dbl>
##  1 Lactobacillus   3306159
##  2 Lactococcus      836381
##  3 Staphylococcus   469170
##  4 Weissella        378415
##  5 Leuconostoc      322343
##  6 Exiguobacterium  165224
##  7 Enterobacter     146900
##  8 Enterococcus     131185
##  9 Streptococcus    116391
## 10 Pseudomonas      107293

Lactobacillus alone accounts for more than half of all counts.

Plots

Library size per sample

Totals span more than two orders of magnitude, so the y-axis uses a log scale: otherwise the shallow samples would be invisible.

ggplot(library_sizes, aes(x = reorder(Sample, Total), y = Total)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Library size per sample",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total counts (log10 scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 6))

Top 10 genera by total abundance

reorder() sorts the bars by abundance, and coord_flip() makes them horizontal so the genus names are easy to read.

ggplot(top_genera, aes(x = reorder(Genus, Total), y = Total)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 genera by total abundance",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total counts (all samples)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

Relative abundance per sample

Converting counts to percentages removes the effect of unequal sequencing depth and makes community composition comparable across samples. The stacked bars show the top 8 genera; the composition differences between samples are striking: some are almost pure Lactobacillus, others are dominated by Lactococcus or by Leuconostoc/Weissella.

top8 <- top_genera$Genus[1:8]

composition <- tidy_counts |>
  mutate(RelAbundance = 100 * Count / sum(Count), .by = Sample) |>
  filter(Genus %in% top8) |>
  # Sort genera in the legend by overall abundance
  mutate(Genus = factor(Genus, levels = rev(top8)))

ggplot(composition, aes(x = Sample, y = RelAbundance, fill = Genus)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 8 genera: relative abundance per sample",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Relative abundance (%)",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 6),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

Recap

Step Key functions
Import read_tsv(), rename()
Reshape pivot_longer()
Parse taxonomy str_extract(), str_remove(), replace_na()
Summarize summarise(.by = ...), arrange(), slice_head()
Transform mutate() (incl. grouped with .by), filter()
Plot ggplot() + geom_col(), scale_y_log10(), coord_flip()
